# Hallmark **A design skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode that refuses to look AI-generated.** [usehallmark.com](https://www.usehallmark.com)  ·  forty-eight themes  ·  custom on request  ·  redesign and audit by name Made by Together AI.

Hallmark holds a hard floor and then gets out of the way. It deals three themes from a catalog of forty-eight materials, builds the page around what the visitor came to do, and lints the result in a real browser against the tells that read as machine-made: the eyebrow above every heading, tracked-capital labels, one coloured word in a headline, a page of empty frames or nothing but photographs, a hero that misses its screen, an email sign-up at the end of every page, a form that says thanks without sending anything. A fresh-context reviewer gets the last word. The gates come in tiers. The **Floor** never ships (contrast, focus, reduced motion, invented facts, a broken phone layout). **Reflex** gates are the defaults a model falls into; a build with a reason may overrule one on the record. **Finish** checks are craft detail that never blocks a ship. ## New in v2 - **Forty-eight themes.** Each is a material (paper, type, colour, surfaces, its own components and texture) with a picture of a finished page, and the build lays out its own page in it. - **Built from the job.** A booking page books, a shop sells, a newsletter subscribes: the action sits where the category puts it, and the page ends on it. - **Custom.** Ask for a custom page and Hallmark designs from your prompt alone, under the same rules and checks. - **Your real product.** Point it at a URL, a dev server or an app and it captures the screenshots itself. - **Real photographs.** 755 openly licensed photos, picked per subject and credited on the page. - **Redesign and audit.** `/hallmark redesign ` rebuilds a page and keeps its content and wiring; `/hallmark audit ` only reports. ## Themes
Dusk
Closewise, bank reconciliation		 Cobalt
Relay, a webhook API		 Studio
Field Office, an identity studio		 Atelier
Maison Orla, a fragrance atelier		 Ribbon
Lull, a sleep sounds app
Furrow
Fieldbook, farm records		 Dose
Tandem, a family medication app		 Hum
Sprout, a reading game for kids		 Terminal
burrow, a dotfiles CLI		 Hedgerow
Five Mile Gin, a distillery
Ten of the forty-eight. A theme is a material, not a plan: it never says what a page contains or in what order, so two prompts in one theme make two different pages. Each is one file of at most 8 KB in [`references/themes/`](skills/hallmark/references/themes/) with a picture beside it; a build reads exactly one. See them all at [usehallmark.com](https://www.usehallmark.com). ## Custom Say **custom** and Hallmark drops the themes: no plan, no components, no palette recipe, only the floor, the gates and a short direction in [`direction.md`](skills/hallmark/references/direction.md) to find one idea that only this client has and let it run the page. ## How a build runs 1. Pre-flight reads the project (fonts, palette, framework, a locked `design.md`) and asks once for the material: photos, screenshots, real numbers. Nothing is invented. 2. `scripts/theme.mjs deal` offers three themes that fit the prompt and clear the log; `draw` deals the page's anatomy from its job. 3. The hero is built alone, rendered and reviewed cold before the rest of the page exists. 4. `scripts/sloplint.mjs --render` checks the page at eight widths, then a subagent reviews it with fresh eyes. Each page is self-contained HTML and CSS, stamped in its first CSS comment with the decisions it took. ## Redesign Hallmark never starts on a design that already exists unless you name it: ``` /hallmark redesign ./src/app /hallmark audit ./index.html ``` A full redesign keeps the content and the wiring and changes the system and the layout; say *keep the layout* for a restyle or *polish* for only the tells. `sloplint --before` records every link, field, handler and heading first, `sloplint --kept` fails the redesign if one went missing, and the handoff is a side-by-side before and after. ## Install ``` npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g ``` `-g` installs for every project; leave it off to install into the current one. Needs Node 18 or later. The browser checks (`sloplint --render`, screenshots) also need `npm i -g puppeteer-core` and Chrome; without them the static checks still run. | Harness | Lands in | Invoke | | --- | --- | --- | | Claude Code | `~/.claude/skills/hallmark` | `/hallmark ` or describe a new build | | Codex CLI | `~/.agents/skills/hallmark` | `$hallmark ` or describe a new build | | Cursor | finds the copies above | `/hallmark ` or describe a new build | | OpenCode | finds the copies above | `/hallmark ` or describe a new build | - **One harness only:** `npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g --agent claude-code` (or `codex`, `opencode`, `cursor`, `github-copilot`). - **As a Claude Code plugin:** `/plugin marketplace add nutlope/hallmark`, then `/plugin install hallmark@hallmark` (invoked as `/hallmark:hallmark`). - **From a clone:** `node skills/hallmark/scripts/install.mjs` validates every theme and reference before it copies; `install-hook.mjs` adds an edit-time Floor check to Claude Code. - **Lint any page:** `node skills/hallmark/scripts/sloplint.mjs --render`. - **If it does not fire on its own,** name it: *use hallmark to build ...*. ## Licence MIT. Use it, fork it, ship it. The photo library (`skills/hallmark/scripts/photos.json`) lists photographs hosted on Wikimedia Commons and holds no image files. Each keeps its own licence (CC0, public domain, CC BY or CC BY-SA), and Hallmark credits every one it uses on the page. It does not use stock sites (Unsplash, Pexels, Pixabay), whose terms bar AI tools from picking their images.

details.readme:
# security-audit

A coding-agent skill that turns your agent into a security auditor. It orchestrates isolated agents through reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting.

This is the skill that seeded Cloudflare's vulnerability discovery harness, described in [Build your own vulnerability harness](https://blog.cloudflare.com/build-your-own-vulnerability-harness). The harness grew into a multi-stage, fleet-wide system; this skill is the single-repo starting point it evolved from.

## What it does

The skill runs a structured audit in six phases:

1. **Reconnaissance** -- map architecture, trust boundaries, input surfaces, prior evidence, and deterministic coverage in `architecture.md` and `coverage-ledger.json`.
2. **Coverage-led hunting** -- assign isolated hunters from ledger units, record their checks, and use coverage critics to find gaps.
3. **Candidate validation** -- give every unique candidate to a fresh verifier that tries to disprove it.
4. **Structured output** -- write `confirmed`, `needs_validation`, and `rejected` records to `findings.json` and validate them against `report-schema.json`.
5. **Independent record verification** -- fresh agents verify final source claims. Material replacements receive another independent verifier.
6. **Target-neutral reporting** -- derive `REPORT.md`, `FINDINGS-DETAIL.md`, and `NEEDS-VALIDATION.md` from the verified records and coverage ledger.

The parent runs `validate-coverage-ledger.cjs` after creating the ledger and after each later ledger update. It runs `validate-findings.cjs` in Phase 4 and again after every Phase 5 replacement.

The verdicts are distinct: `confirmed` has a complete source trace and bounded observed result, `needs_validation` has an exact unresolved fact and no severity, and `rejected` records a disproved candidate.

Multiple runs against the same repo are additive. The skill uses prior ledgers and findings to target gaps, revalidate changed source, and carry forward current-source evidence without treating stale or unresolved work as covered.

## Files

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `SKILL.md` | Setup, core principles, platform terminology, workflow overview, and audit anti-patterns |
| `RECONNAISSANCE.md` | Phase 1 reconnaissance prompts and synthesis instructions |
| `HUNTING.md` | Phase 2 orchestration, hunting methodology, and validation rules |
| `ATTACK-CLASSES.md` | Core, wildcard, and obvious-things attack prompts |
| `MEMORY-SAFETY-AND-BINARY.md` | Memory-safety, binary, and kernel hunting classes for native targets |
| `AI-AND-LLM.md` | Prompt-injection, agent/tool, and output-handling hunting classes for LLM-backed targets |
| `WEB-PROTOCOL-AND-AUTH.md` | HTTP request-framing, cache, and authentication-protocol hunting classes for HTTP-protocol and auth targets |
| `CLIENT-SIDE.md` | DOM-injection, messaging-trust, UI-redress, and prototype-pollution hunting classes for client-side/browser targets |
| `SUPPLY-CHAIN-AND-RELEASE.md` | Dependency, CI, release, signing, update, plugin, and extension hunting classes |
| `CLOUD-AND-DEPLOYMENT.md` | IAM, infrastructure-as-code, container, serverless, ingress, and runtime-configuration hunting classes |
| `PROTOCOLS-RPC-AND-MESSAGING.md` | RPC, serialization, queue, broker, webhook, and streaming-protocol hunting classes |
| `RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION-AND-AVAILABILITY.md` | Shared resource, quota, queue, worker, and operator-spend hunting classes |
| `DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE.md` | Tenant isolation, cache, search, export, backup, migration, deletion, and restore hunting classes |
| `DESKTOP-MOBILE-AND-LOCAL-IPC.md` | Native app, deep-link, webview, exported-component, helper, daemon, and local-IPC hunting classes |
| `VALIDATION-AND-REPORTING.md` | Phases 3–6 candidate validation, structured output, record verification, and reporting |
| `report-schema.json` | JSON schema for all three `findings.json` verdicts |
| `validate-findings.cjs` | Zero-dependency validator for `findings.json` in Phases 4 and 5 |
| `validate-findings.test.cjs` | Findings-validator tests and producer-compatible fixture checks |
| `validate-coverage-ledger.cjs` | Zero-dependency validator for `coverage-ledger.json` in Phases 1–5 |
| `validate-coverage-ledger.test.cjs` | Coverage-ledger validator tests |

## Installation

Install the skill with the [Skills CLI](https://skills.sh):

```bash
npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
  --skill security-audit
```

Use `--global` for a user-level installation:

```bash
npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
  --skill security-audit \
  --global
```

Run `npx skills --help` for agent-selection and non-interactive options.

## Usage

Start your coding agent in (or pointed at) the codebase you want to audit, then ask it to do a security audit:

```
security audit this codebase
```

```
find security vulnerabilities in ./src
```

```
do a security review, output to ~/audits/my-project
```

The skill activates automatically when the request matches its trigger (security audit, find vulnerabilities, pen-test the code, etc.). A direct codebase audit or pen-test request uses full audit mode. Security questions and focused vulnerability work use guidance mode unless you request report artifacts. In full audit mode, an unspecified output directory defaults to `~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>`. The workflow writes inside the target repository only when you explicitly select a directory that version control ignores.

## Requirements

- A coding agent with a model that supports tool use and parallel sub-agents
- Node.js for the zero-dependency findings and coverage-ledger validators
- An OS-enforced sandbox for target-controlled builds, tests, processes, browsers, emulators, fuzzers, and fixtures. It must disable external networking, use a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforce resource limits, and allow writes only to assigned scratch paths. Without these controls, the workflow keeps the lead as `needs_validation` instead of executing target code.

## Design principles

- **Only confirm established boundary failures.** Keep a source-grounded blocked lead as `needs_validation` with its exact unresolved fact.
- **Adversarial validation.** The agent that checks a finding is never the agent that found it.
- **Severity requires impact.** Likelihood x impact, not deviation from a checklist.
- **Defense-in-depth gaps are not vulnerabilities.** If Layer A prevents the attack, the absence of Layer B is a hardening note.
- **Multiple runs improve coverage.** In our test runs, a single run found roughly half of the vulnerabilities that repeated runs found in total.

## Contact

Questions, feedback, or comparing notes on AI-driven security tooling: security-ai-research@cloudflare.com

## License

# ThinkRail [![JetBrains incubator project](https://jb.gg/badges/incubator-plastic.svg)](https://confluence.jetbrains.com/display/ALL/JetBrains+on+GitHub) [![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/JetBrains/thinkrail?style=social)](https://star-history.com/#JetBrains/thinkrail&Date) ThinkRail is the agentic IDE that gets better every time you use it — learning your project through living specs today, and building its own capabilities tomorrow. We built a rich interface around the [`pi`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent) coding agent, isolated work into separate workspaces, and gave the agent durable project knowledge through living specs and reusable skills. Next, we're adding full extension support, so ThinkRail can create the tools it needs based on how you actually work. **Website:** [thinkrail.ai](https://thinkrail.ai/) · **Blog:** [thinkrail.ai/blog](https://thinkrail.ai/blog/) ⭐ If you find ThinkRail useful, give it a star — it helps others discover it. *A `pi` session and the change it made, scoped to an isolated git-worktree workspace.* ## What you get - **Isolated workspaces.** Open any git repo as a project and cut workspaces from it as `git worktree`s, each with its own branch and working directory. Agents work in parallel without touching your checkout; merge the good branch, delete the rest. You can also attach existing worktrees or explicitly work in the project folder itself. Finished and dormant workspaces settle onto a per-project shelf on their own — when their pull request merges or closes, or after a quiet week — and come back the moment you work in them. The topbar shows where the active branch stands against `origin` and its pull request, with the next step one click away: publish, push, or open a PR described from the plan, the commits, your PR template, or an agent-written draft. Once a GitHub PR is open it shows the CI checks and review decision, and lets you mark it ready, hand failing checks or a diverged branch to the agent, merge it with the repository's last-used method, reopen it, or delete the remote branch. - **A real IDE around the agent.** A splittable workbench of Monaco editor tabs, a Files tree with live git change marks and a Changed view, terminals, and documents — all scoped to the active workspace. Leave anchored review comments on files and diffs and send them to a chat as structured context, or open the worktree in your installed IDE. - **Chats that stream like the engine thinks.** Several concurrent `pi` sessions per workspace, each with its own model and live token and cost readout. Steer a running turn or queue a follow-up, delegate to subagents, and work a shared plan the agent updates and you edit — each completed step can be committed and reviewed on its own. - **Specs as ground truth.** A connected graph of `SPEC.md` files lives beside the code; the agent reads, searches, and maintains it through dedicated `spec_*` tools, so intent survives the session. The read-only Specs tool renders the graph as a tree in the workbench. - **Skills and workflows.** Portable Agent Skills you already keep for other coding agents are read in place, and bundled workflows guide project setup, design brainstorming, and shipping a pull request — pushing the workspace branch and opening or updating its GitHub PR through your own `gh`. - **Agent tools beyond the shell.** Web research, and inline diagrams, option comparisons and file previews rendered right in the chat — when the agent proposes a UI change it shows a before/after mockup you can comment on like a diff. Settings → Extensions lists the ThinkRail extensions the agent gets and lets you switch each one off. - **MCP servers.** Connect the MCP servers in your `pi` `mcp.json` (or add them, and a few presets, from Settings): ThinkRail asks in the chat before calls the server does not mark read-only (or always allows the tools you trust in a project), keeps servers a repository defines off until you approve them, signs you in to OAuth servers from Settings, and shows each chat's servers next to its background commands and subagents. - **Your providers, your credentials.** Sign in with [JetBrains AI](https://www.jetbrains.com/ai/) or connect any provider through `pi`'s own auth. ThinkRail has no accounts of its own. - **Desktop app or browser.** A native desktop app, or the `thinkrail` CLI that opens the same app in your browser. Both embed the same engine host; app state lives under `~/.thinkrail`. - **Your language.** Settings → Language follows your system language or a language you pick; English and Simplified Chinese are built in. Add a language ThinkRail doesn't ship yet by dropping a translated `en.json` into `~/.thinkrail/locales` — it applies as you save. Agent replies and tool output stay as the agent wrote them. *The project's spec graph as a tree, with the spec itself rendered alongside.* ## Install ThinkRail ships in two additive forms: a native desktop installer and the self-contained `thinkrail` CLI. Both are published with `SHA256SUMS` on the [releases page](https://github.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/releases). ### Desktop Download the `thinkrail-desktop-*` asset for your platform: - **macOS (Apple Silicon)** — open the DMG. There is no Intel desktop build. - **Windows x64** — extract the complete setup ZIP, then run its setup executable in place, next to its payload. - **Linux x64 / ARM64** — extract the setup tarball and run `installer`. Desktop builds need glibc 2.38+ with GTK 3, WebKitGTK 4.1, Ayatana AppIndicator 3, and librsvg 2 — Ubuntu 24.04 or newer: ```bash sudo apt install libgtk-3-0 libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 libayatana-appindicator3-1 librsvg2-2 ``` Packaged stable and nightly desktop builds check for updates in the background and offer them in **Settings → Updates**: **Download** → **Preparing update** → **Install & Restart**. Nothing is applied until you choose **Install & Restart**. ThinkRail then shows the installation's progress and log, closes, and reopens on the new version. After the restart it tells you whether the update installed. If it didn't, it explains why and offers to retry. The updater appears only when the package carries a valid HTTPS feed identity; installations that predate that identity need one manual installation first. ### Command line The installer downloads the right binary, verifies its SHA-256 checksum, and puts `thinkrail` on your PATH. **macOS / Linux** (also Windows under Git Bash): ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash ``` **Windows** — the same command works from cmd and PowerShell: ```powershell powershell -c "irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex" ``` Then run `thinkrail`, optionally with a git repo to open as a project: ```bash thinkrail ~/code/my-repo ``` `thinkrail` needs `git` on your PATH and a model provider — sign in with JetBrains AI from the app or use your own provider credentials. `thinkrail --help` lists the flags; `thinkrail --version` prints the build.
Nightly builds, pinned versions, updates, and uninstall The installer takes `--channel stable|nightly` and `--version`; a pinned version must belong to the selected channel: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel stable --version 0.1.2 curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly --version 0.2.0-nightly.10 ``` On Windows the options are environment variables (`THINKRAIL_CHANNEL`, `THINKRAIL_VERSION`, `THINKRAIL_PREFIX`, `THINKRAIL_NO_MODIFY_PATH`): ```powershell $env:THINKRAIL_CHANNEL='nightly'; irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex # PowerShell set "THINKRAIL_CHANNEL=stable" && set "THINKRAIL_VERSION=0.1.2" && powershell -c "irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex" # cmd ``` Installed stable and nightly CLI hosts periodically offer **Run Update** in **Settings → Updates**. It runs the host machine's `thinkrail update` in the background — also when the UI is open in a browser on another machine — and a successful update asks you to restart the host manually. You can run `thinkrail update` directly on any platform: it re-runs the installer for the installed channel and replaces `/bin/thinkrail[.exe]`; pass `--channel` or `--version` only for an explicit override. `thinkrail uninstall` removes the executable, the PATH entry the installer added, and the install metadata, and asks whether to delete your `~/.thinkrail` app state (kept by default — `--remove-data` deletes it, `-y` skips the questions). Prefer a manual install? Download a binary and `SHA256SUMS` from the releases page and verify the checksum. For self-update to work, rename it to `thinkrail` (`thinkrail.exe` on Windows) and place it at `/bin/thinkrail[.exe]`; a binary kept under its release filename or elsewhere must be replaced manually or reinstalled with the script.
### Platform notes | Platform | Desktop | CLI | | --- | --- | --- | | macOS Apple Silicon | DMG | signed binary | | macOS Intel | no Electrobun build | not prebuilt — [build from source](#developing-thinkrail) | | Windows x64 | signed setup executable and app binaries | signed `.exe` | | Linux x64 / ARM64 | setup tarball, unsigned | unsigned | JetBrains signs the Windows CLI, the desktop setup executable, and every executable and DLL the desktop app installs. The macOS CLI is signed but not yet notarized. Signed and notarized desktop DMGs require the coordinated JetBrains service pipeline; older published DMGs and locally built packages may still be unsigned and blocked by Gatekeeper. Linux artifacts are unsigned. ## Analytics & privacy ThinkRail collects basic usage events — launches, chat creation, message sends, provider connections — tied to a random installation ID. Usage analytics never include prompts, code, files, credentials, or account identity. Error reports are also always sent, tied to the same installation ID, so we can fix crashes: the error type and code and where in ThinkRail's own code it happened. They never include error messages, file paths, names, URLs, or anything from your projects or extensions. Additional product usage and how you found ThinkRail are shared only while **Share additional usage data** is on; the switch is offered at first launch and lives in **Settings → Privacy**. When launching from the command line, `thinkrail --no-analytics` (or `THINKRAIL_NO_ANALYTICS=1`) turns additional sharing off for that run. details.readme:
Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.

Studio | Quickstart | Showcase | Playground | Catalog | Docs | Discord

HyperFrames is an open-source framework for turning HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into deterministic MP4 videos. Use it locally with the CLI, from AI coding agents with skills, or as the rendering core behind hosted authoring workflows. Using Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or another coding agent? Run `npx hyperframes skills update` once, then ask your agent to make a video. ## Quick Start ### With an AI coding agent For Claude Code, install the versioned plugin: ```bash claude plugin marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes ``` To enable auto-update for the **hyperframes** marketplace, run `claude` in a terminal in your project. In Claude Code's terminal UI, run `/plugin`, then select **Marketplaces** → **hyperframes** → **Enable auto-update**. Afterward, use `/hyperframes:hyperframes`. See the [plugin guide](docs/guides/plugins.mdx) for Copilot, VS Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, updates, and migration. For standalone skills (including OpenCode), use: ```bash npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes ``` > The picker opens with nothing pre-selected — the **Core Skills** group is all you need; `/slideshow`, `/remotion-to-hyperframes` and `/figma` install on demand. Agents and non-interactive runs should use `npx hyperframes skills update` instead — it installs exactly the core set, whereas `skills add --all` installs all 7 published skills. The six repo-internal skills under `.claude/skills` / `.agents/skills` are excluded by default. For the full published set use `npx hyperframes skills`. > > `skills add` resolves the skills.sh registry blob, which can lag `main` by hours. `npx hyperframes skills update` installs from the current `main`, so reach for it when you need the newest copy of a skill. Run project-local installs from your video project's directory. From a HyperFrames checkout, use `npx hyperframes skills update` for a global install instead: a project-local installer target can overlap the tracked `skills/` source and overwrite uncommitted edits. See [contributor setup](CONTRIBUTING.md#getting-started). Try a prompt like: > Using `/hyperframes`, create a 10-second product intro with a fade-in title, a background video, and subtle background music. The skills teach agents the HyperFrames production loop: plan the video, write valid HTML, wire seekable animations, add media, lint, preview, and render. They work with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, IBM Bob, and other coding agents that support skills. ## Skills HyperFrames ships 7 skills. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (film, captions, overlays, motion, look). Read it first. For standalone installation, default to the **core set** (`/hyperframes`, `/hyperframes-cli`, `/hyperframes-registry`, `/media-use`). `npx hyperframes skills update` installs exactly that from anywhere; the interactive picker (`npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes`) lists it as the "Core Skills" group, nothing pre-selected. The picker is interactive-only — a non-interactive or agent run without `--skill` installs all 7. Use `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --all` to install the complete published set deliberately (skips the picker), or `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --skill ` for just one (bare name, no leading `/`). Standalone installs stay lean after that: `npx hyperframes init` installs the **core set** only when it is missing and never touches a skill you already have (`npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes them, and never removes one); `/figma`, `/slideshow` and `/remotion-to-hyperframes` install **on demand** with `npx hyperframes skills update `. Nothing re-pulls the full set behind your back. ### Plugin packages Plugins bundle the full skill catalog and use their agent's update manager. `bun run package:agent-plugin` builds the committed portable ZIP, source metadata, and SHA-256 checksum. See the [maintainer checklist](docs/contributing/agent-plugins.mdx). ### Upload to Codex Build the upload-ready Codex plugin archive from the committed `HEAD` version of the manifest, brand assets, and skills: ```bash bun run package:codex-plugin ``` This writes `dist/hyperframes-plugin.zip` with a `hyperframes/` root folder and fails if the archive exceeds Codex's 100 MB upload limit. ### Core set | Skill | Use when | | ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `/hyperframes` | **Read first** for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays with HyperFrames (HTML rendered to video). Holds the render contract and the work loop, and points to the references for format, motion, look, captions, whole films and storyboards. | | `/hyperframes-cli` | The HyperFrames CLI by job — scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render locally or in the cloud, publish, project history — plus reading its JSON and recovering from build or render failures. | | `/hyperframes-registry` | About 450 ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source — transitions, overlays, titles, kinetic type, captions, charts, maps, 3D, camera moves. Use before hand-building any named visual; also for `hyperframes add` and `catalog`. | | `/media-use` | Get or make any media for a video — music, sound effects, images, icons, logos, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades and looks — with HeyGen or free local tools, and mix placed audio. Also for footage that looks dark, flat or dull. | ### On demand | Skill | Use when | | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `/figma` | Bring Figma into a video — rendered assets, brand tokens, components, storyboard frames as reconstructed motion, shaders and connector-assisted motion. Use when you paste a figma.com link. | | `/slideshow` | A presentation, pitch deck or interactive deck — discrete slides, fragment reveals, branching, hotspot navigation, presenter mode with speaker notes. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4. | | `/remotion-to-hyperframes` | Bringing existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, other tools' renders), verified frame by frame. | For visual design handoff workflows, see the [Claude Design guide](https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/claude-design) and [Open Design guide](https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/open-design). ### Manually with the CLI ```bash npx hyperframes init my-video cd my-video npx hyperframes preview # preview in browser with live reload npx hyperframes render # render to MP4 ``` **Requirements:** Node.js 22+, FFmpeg ## What You Can Build Need ideas? Browse the [Showcase](https://hyperframes.heygen.com/showcase) for finished videos you can watch, read, run, and remix. - Product launch videos and feature announcements - PR walkthroughs with animated code diffs, narration, and captions - Data visualizations, chart races, and map animations - Social videos with kinetic captions, overlays, and music - Docs-to-video, PDF-to-video, and site-tour explainers - Reusable motion graphics for automated content pipelines ## Frame.md **frame.md — your design system, ready for video.** Every brand has a `design.md`. None of them were written for a camera. `frame.md` is the missing translation layer: it takes your web-context design spec and inverts it for the frame — the same tokens, the same rules, but rewritten so an AI agent can compose a promo video without guessing at scale or reaching for web chrome. The output is a `DESIGN.md` superset your whole toolchain can read. Atoms stay sacred. Composition stays free. Numbers come from the script.

details.readme:
# Speech Studio **Free, offline AI voice studio for Windows — voice any text with cloned and built-in voices, and turn recordings into text with the speakers. Russian done right: numbers in their cases, stress marks, «ё» and homographs. 100% local, zero Python: one native `.exe` (Rust + C++/CUDA); every model and engine downloads with a button.** [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/timoncool/speech-studio?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/timoncool/speech-studio?style=flat-square)](https://github.com/timoncool/speech-studio/stargazers) [![Latest release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/timoncool/speech-studio?include_prereleases&style=flat-square)](https://github.com/timoncool/speech-studio/releases) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/github/downloads/timoncool/speech-studio/total?style=flat-square)](https://github.com/timoncool/speech-studio/releases) [![Last commit](https://img.shields.io/github/last-commit/timoncool/speech-studio?style=flat-square)](https://github.com/timoncool/speech-studio/commits) **English** · [Русский](README.ru.md) · [中文](README.zh.md) · [Español](README.es.md) · [Português](README.pt.md) · [Français](README.fr.md) ![Speech Studio — a voiced dialog with a voice per character](docs/screenshots/en-01-speech.webp)
## What it is **Speech Studio** has three modes. **Speech** voices text: a line, a dialog with a voice per character, a podcast the director writes for you, or a whole book from EPUB, FB2, PDF or DOCX. **Listening** turns a recording, a video or a link into text with who said what and when, cuts it by its words, checks a voicing against the text it should say and makes library voices from its speakers. **Live** is a voice conversation with an AI agent connected over MCP: it says each phrase as soon as it writes it and hears you through the microphone. Everything runs **locally on your machine** — no cloud, no subscription; your texts, recordings and voiceprints never leave your computer. If you want a voice your card can't run, the cloud voices of **OpenRouter**, **Google Gemini**, **fal.ai** and **Runware** are there too, each behind its own key and a confirmation before the first call; they are off by default. It's a **fully native app**: no embeddable Python, no torch, no CUDA wheels. The whole studio is **Rust + native C++/CUDA engines (GGUF/ONNX)** in one process. Models, engines, the CUDA and VC++ runtimes and ffmpeg are **downloaded by the app itself** on first run, and a model another of the author's studios already has is taken from it instead of downloaded again. **An NVIDIA GPU is what the app is built and tested for**; see *What runs where* for the rest. ## For AI agents While Speech Studio is open it serves MCP at `http://127.0.0.1:8797/mcp`: an agent such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or Codex does everything the window does, through the same code — voices a text into a file in one call, makes and edits projects block by block, casts voices to characters, designs a voice from a description, transcribes and checks recordings, exports audiobooks with chapters and subtitles. Settings, **Agent (MCP)** shows whether an agent is connected and what to paste into the client. The one thing an agent cannot do is turn the microphone on: Live, a recording and the microphone test start only on your own click or key. 1. Install the studio from the [latest release](https://github.com/timoncool/speech-studio/releases/latest) and start it. 2. Connect to its MCP server: ```bash claude mcp add --transport http speech-studio http://127.0.0.1:8797/mcp ``` Other clients: `{ "mcpServers": { "speech-studio": { "type": "streamable-http", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8797/mcp" } } }` 3. Read the skill the server serves (resource `studio://skill`), the same text as [docs/mcp-skill.md](docs/mcp-skill.md), and start with the tool `studio_status`. The studio also speaks the OpenAI audio API on the same port — `POST /v1/audio/speech`, `POST /v1/audio/transcriptions`, `GET /v1/models` — so tools written for OpenAI voice and transcribe through it, with a library voice's name as `voice`. [llms.txt](llms.txt) says the same for tools that look for it. Only programs on this computer may connect. ## What you can make with it - **An audiobook** — drop an EPUB or FB2: chapters, characters with their own voices, an M4B with chapters and cover, ACX loudness checked. - **A podcast or a dialog** — the director writes a podcast on a topic for two or three speakers, or paste lines like «Anna: …»; the timeline shows every overlap. - **A voice-over for a video** — voice a script or subtitles into their cues, lay music and sounds under it in the track editor, export at the video's loudness. - **A transcript of an interview or a lecture** — who said what and when, word times, subtitles by broadcasters' rules, the recording cut by its text. - **A check of a dubbing** — lay the script over the recording and see every word said wrong or skipped. - **Your own voice library** — record or import voices, clean them, make voices from the speakers of a recording. - **A voice for your AI agent** — talk with Claude Code or any MCP agent in Live, or let it voice and transcribe files through MCP or the OpenAI-compatible API. Examples of every engine and voice, with Russian stress before and after, are on the [project page](https://timoncool.github.io/speech-studio/). ## Three modes | Mode | What it does | |------|--------------| | 🔊 **Speech** | Text, dialog, podcast or book → voiced blocks with takes, checked by ear, exported as WAV, FLAC, MP3, OGG, M4A or M4B with chapters, subtitles and synced text | | 👂 **Listening** | Audio, video or a link → a transcript with speakers and word times, a karaoke player, cut-by-text, export to SRT, VTT, ASS, TXT or JSON, a check against a reference text | | 🎙️ **Live** | A voice conversation with an AI agent: the agent connected over MCP speaks each phrase as it writes it, you answer into the microphone and are recognised phrase by phrase, a phrase said over it stops it; only you turn the microphone on, pause with M or Ctrl+Shift+Space, a widget over every window | ## Features **Voices and engines** - **Five local engines** — [Higgs Audio v3](https://huggingface.co/bosonai) (cloning, emotions and sounds), **Fish Audio Drama 3** (the strongest open voice; the whole model on a 24 GB card, from 6 GB with its experts in RAM), **Supertonic 3** (fast, ten built-in voices), **Qwen3-TTS 1.7B** (nine built-in voices, cloning, an instruction per block) and **Qwen3-TTS with Russian stress**, siriusfreak's LoRA applied at run time. - **Engine per character and per block** over the project's own; an engine that can't speak the voice in use says which of its voices it takes. - **Voice library** — a voice pack in one click, 743 Russian voices from the cloud catalogue, recording from the microphone, import of files and ZIPs, photo, gender, age, language, tags and consent; the reference transcript is recognised once and kept. - **Clean a reference** — Mel-Band Roformer takes the voice from music, **DPDFNet** takes noise away with a strength control so speech stays alive; the original is kept. - **Best piece of a reference** — windows at pauses between recognised words, each with its length, signal-to-noise, clipping and longest pause. - **Voice by description** — Qwen3-TTS VoiceDesign makes a voice from "an elderly woman with a soft, slightly hoarse voice…": hear several candidates, keep one in the library. - **Cloud voices** — OpenRouter, Google Gemini (parallel requests or Batch at half the price), fal.ai and Runware, each behind its own key and a confirmation before the first call. **Text that sounds right** - **Russian normaliser** — numbers in the right case and gender, dates, times, money, units, Roman numerals, Latin brand names and abbreviations. - **Stress, «ё» and homographs** by RUAccent — the large homograph model (big_poetry in int8, the same choices as fp32) picks замо́к or за́мок by the sentence; doubtful ones are highlighted for you, your own `+` marks stay. - **Pronunciation dictionary** — replace, regex and phonemes, scoped to the project, a language, a voice or an engine, Balabolka `.rex`/`.dic`/`.bxd` import, and a check by ear right from the dictionary. - **SpeechKit-compatible markup** — `+` stress, `sil<[300]>` and `[pause 500ms]` pauses, `[rate:1.2]` tempo, `**accent**`; what an engine ignores is marked, never silently dropped. - **More of the text read right** — an SSML subset, prosody hints coloured word by word, phone numbers, e-mail addresses and codes, a passage in another language in the same voice, and a check of the script before voicing. **Projects** - **Text as the timeline** — blocks with speakers, takes (up to five), stale tracking, undo and redo, drag to reorder, search and replace with regex, notes and markers. - **Quality control** — every take recognised back and compared word by word, plus checks for clipping, silence, cut-off, a click at the end, a repeated phrase, a long tail, music or noise instead of speech, and similarity to the reference voice; several takes with the best one picked. - **Dialog and podcasts** — `Anna:` and `[Anna]` lines become characters, the director writes a podcast on a topic for N speakers, negative pauses make interruptions, and the **timeline** shows every overlap with cut, join or keep. - **Audiobooks** — EPUB, FB2, PDF, DOCX, HTML, Markdown and TXT with chapter preview, cast by the director, M4B with chapters and cover, parts for long books, ACX loudness check. - **Subtitles as a project** — SRT, VTT and ASS lines voiced into their cues: the tempo raised ahead, a retry when a take doesn't fit, then stretching and borrowing the silence before the line. - **Export check** — blocks missing, stale, failed, with a changed file or too long for their cue are listed before export; only the length may be allowed through. - **Loudness** — video (−14 LUFS), podcast (−16 LUFS) and ACX presets with a true-peak limiter, room tone and breaths between blocks. - **Project file** — `.speechproj` with text, voices and audio carries a project to another computer. - **Montage** — a track editor under the text: move, trim, fade and level each clip, music and sound tracks from files or folders, or a song made right there in YuE2, MiniMax Music3 or ACE-Step Studio. - **Export for every use** — a file per chapter, a track per character in a ZIP, a CSV table of lines, voice effects (radio, phone, loudspeaker), even loudness of pieces, sample rate and bit depth, file name templates, a SHA-256 manifest and a note on how it was made. - **Compare and approve** — A/B of takes, a blind comparison of engines on the same text, approved blocks a re-voicing leaves alone, a quality traffic light and a project report. - **Books and plays** — direct speech apart from the author's, a cast of characters with voices picked for them, footnotes cleaned out, the book's names into the dictionary, a project updated from a corrected book without losing what is voiced, and an HTML player of the book. **Listening** - **Parakeet-TDT and Nemotron 3.5 (28 languages with punctuation) on transcribe.cpp, or Whisper**, up to eight speakers by Nemotron 3 Diarization, a long recording cut at pauses by **Silero VAD v6**, noise removed by DPDFNet, music removed by Roformer. - **A hint for Whisper** — topic and spellings, plus the corrections you add. - **Batch** — drop several files at once; each becomes a recording queued for recognition. - **Lay a known text over the recording** — the reference text takes the time of each heard word, sentence by sentence. - **Voices from speakers** — a library voice from each speaker's cleanest words. - **As you speak** — recognition from the microphone phrase by phrase, a watched folder recognised in t

YuE2 Studio is a desktop studio for **YuE2**, the open song model from M-A-P that writes a score before it sings. Describe a style, write the lyrics, and the model composes a melody with chords as sheet music, then performs it as a full song with vocals. The score comes back with the track: read it, edit it, and render the same composition again with a different sound. Windows installer with auto-update or a portable folder, runs offline on an NVIDIA card with 6 GB of VRAM or more; AMD and Intel cards through Vulkan are experimental. It is built on [yue2.cpp](https://github.com/ServeurpersoCom/yue2.cpp), the native C++/CUDA port of YuE2. The studio around it is Rust and React in a Tauri window — nothing in the runtime path is Python. ## For AI agents Given this repository, an agent can set everything up and drive the studio by itself: 1. Install the studio from the [latest release](https://github.com/timoncool/YuE2-Studio/releases/latest) and start it. 2. Connect to its MCP server at `http://127.0.0.1:8791/mcp`: `claude mcp add --transport http yue2-studio http://127.0.0.1:8791/mcp` 3. Read the skill it serves (resource `studio://skill`, prompt `studio`), the same text as [docs/mcp-skill.md](docs/mcp-skill.md), and start with the tool `studio_status`. [llms.txt](llms.txt) says the same for tools that look for it. To keep the skill in Claude Code, save [docs/mcp-skill.md](docs/mcp-skill.md) as `~/.claude/skills/yue2-studio/SKILL.md`. ## What you can do - **A player of its own** — a ten-band equalizer on Winamp's frequencies with its presets, your own and .EQF files; a MilkDrop visualiser with hundreds of presets or a spectrum in ten looks, over the studio, fullscreen or in its own window; and a Winamp mode that turns the whole window into a skinned Winamp 2 whose windows move apart, dock and resize — the original skin and ten more included, sharp at any scale, the Winamp Skin Museum one click away, Ctrl+M to switch. The song, its place and the equalizer carry over both ways. - **Save as, and a Files panel** — songs, stems, MIDI, lyric sheets, scores and videos are saved where you say, in Windows' own Save dialog, and the Files panel shows each save. - **A proxy for the whole studio** — HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5 or SOCKS4, with a login: model downloads, Hugging Face, OpenRouter and updates go through it. - **Full songs from a style and lyrics** — up to ten minutes, in the languages the model sings. In Russian a stress mark (the combining acute U+0301, Alt+0769 on Windows) after a vowel moves the sung stress to it, as Ruach Studio documents. On an RTX 4090 with the Q8_0 set a 3:38 song renders in about 46 seconds. - **Read and edit the score** — the model writes its composition in ABC notation first; the studio engraves it as sheet music. Edit the notes, tempo or key and create again: the composition stays, the performance changes. Or switch to melody-only, or no score at all. - **Compose the score first** — write only the score from the style and lyrics, without singing it (the studio's take on yue2.cpp's `yue-plan`), read and fix it, then create. - **Covers** — SheetSage2 listens to a recording and writes its melody as a score; YuE2 then sings that melody in your style. The words have to fit the melody: the original lyrics work best, new ones need the same syllables line by line with the stresses on the same notes, or the singing drifts off the tune — lines stretch, pause and slide into the wrong section. Transcription mistakes carry into the cover too. A track from your library can be transcribed from its menu. - **Exact replay** — every track keeps its request and its audio codes, so it can be re-rendered bit for bit, or re-rendered with other steps, a new sound seed, several variations, or another output format, without composing again. - **110 ready examples** — the style/lyrics/score sets that ship with yue2.cpp, covers included, one click to load. - **Every engine setting** — all seven sampling knobs (temperature, top-p, top-k, repetition penalty and its window, minimum and maximum tokens) for the score and for the audio codes, flow-matching steps, guidance, both seeds, lossless FLAC or MP3. Prompts open and save as JSON or YAML in the engine's own request format, so they move freely between the studio, the yue2.cpp WebUI and `yue-synth`. - **Structured song writing** — build a style from its musical fields and arrange lyrics in editable sections, while keeping the plain text editable. Give the writing assistant a language, a target of 8–32 lines and additional instructions. - **Song and render controls** — voice and tempo fields; section, line/stanza and text-case tools; Keep/Words lyric preservation and exact checkpoint tokens; batch score-plan selection and chord mirroring in repeated sections. Edit scores with MIDI grid and octave controls. Transpose generation by −24 to +24 semitones, render vocals only through native HT-Demucs as MP3 or 32-bit WAV, and switch each LoRA on or off with weights from −10 to +10. - **A writing assistant** — a local Gemma model or OpenRouter writes the style and lyrics from an idea and edits the score on request; or pick your connected agent (MCP) and it writes instead. Lyrics you wrote yourself get their section tags with one button, the words exactly as you wrote them. - **Word-level karaoke** — enhanced LRC with a timestamp on every word, aligned by Parakeet or Whisper. Your lyrics are kept; only the timing is borrowed. - **Six stems on the GPU** — drums, bass, other, vocals, guitar and piano with HT-Demucs. - **Any track to MIDI** — a song, a stem or a processed take becomes multi-instrument MIDI (34 instrument groups and drums) with MuScriptor on the GPU, through HOT-Step's native port. A piano roll fills in while it listens; play it against the original, mute or solo an instrument, save the .mid. Downloaded the first time it is used. - **A MIDI editor** — a piano roll with tracks, instruments and drums: play a song in from a MIDI keyboard or the computer's keys, record or draw it, edit a track's MIDI, save it to the library as a track and send it to a cover, or open the create form's score in it. A .mid file becomes the score: the voice and instrument chosen, chords read or guessed, karaoke words offered for the lyrics. - **Every result is a track** — stems, a processed take, a re-render and a cover land in the library as tracks of their own, each marked with the one it was made from and keeping the settings it was made with. - **LoRA** — LoRA and LoKr files for either half of the model, the composition or the sound, each with its own strength, picked in the create form. A catalogue of ready ones with their authors credited, and a search on Hugging Face that downloads what you pick. - **Train your own LoRA** — an optional tab on the LoRA page: songs of one artist or style become a LoRA on your own card with HOT-Step's trainer and its tuned recipe (LoKr, Prodigy, lyric timing from a forced aligner that also reads Cyrillic). Every setting of the recipe is editable. Datasets move between this studio and MiniMax Music3 Studio as a folder, and each saved checkpoint goes into the LoRA library in one click. - **A three-step wizard** — drop a folder of songs, check them, train. Albums with a cue sheet are cut into songs; titles and artists come from the tags, the file name and the folders. - **Preparation on its own** — lyrics come from the lyric databases players use (LRCLIB, QQ Music, Kugou), word for word; only a song none of them knows has its vocals separated and is heard by Whisper, with its usual hallucinations filtered out. The assistant lays the lyrics out in sections. MOSS-Music listens to every song and the assistant writes its style, with the tempo measured by Beat This! on the card. - **Every song shows where it is** — the lyrics and styles appear as each song is done, one model on the card at a time, each loaded once for the whole batch. A song that failed or was stopped has a button that finishes just that song. - **Picks up after a restart** — each song keeps what it has; a preparation cut off by a crash or a restart carries on by itself and redoes nothing. - **Stop by drift or by epochs** — stop when the composition half drifts too far from the base, or after a set number of passes over the songs. - **A trigger word from the start** — every dataset gets a rare word made from its name, which you can change. - **Train further** — not there yet at 750 steps? Compare before and after while it plays, then keep the result as a version of the track or throw it away. - **The sound as the model made it** — the engine renders 32-bit float and the studio encodes it once, changing nothing on the way: lossless 24-bit FLAC by default (libFLAC, the reference encoder), MP3 with LAME when you choose it. Normalisation is a stage under Process, after mastering, never part of generation. - **A library of plain files** — search, playlists, cover art from prompt templates, tracks exported with title, lyrics and cover in their own tags (Vorbis comments in a FLAC, ID3 in an MP3). # Horizon Horizon is Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 rewritten in Rust: a native game that reads the same worlds, follows the same rules and generates the same terrain as the Java game, and is checked against it by 281 differential harnesses. You play it through a small launcher, on the files from your own copy of Minecraft. It is free, open source and unofficial. > Not an official Minecraft product. Not approved by or associated with Mojang or Microsoft. Horizon contains no Minecraft code, assets or data: you need your own legally obtained copy of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3. ## Download Horizon is installed through **the Horizon launcher**. Get it from [playhorizon.dev](https://playhorizon.dev) (the Download button picks your system) or from [the launcher releases](https://github.com/ludovic111/horizon/releases?q=launcher-v&expanded=true), for Linux x86-64, macOS on Apple Silicon or Windows x64. The launcher installs and updates the game, prepares its files from your own copy of Minecraft, and updates itself. **You need** Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3, played once (the official launcher, Prism, MultiMC and other launchers all work); a Java 25 runtime, for the one-time preparation; and a GPU with Vulkan on Linux and Windows, or any Apple Silicon Mac. Step by step, with macOS's first-open prompt and the first launch: [Install and first launch](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/install).
## What works today The [documentation](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/) covers each of these. - **The game:** singleplayer with vanilla's world generation, mobs, villagers, raids, redstone, every command, the HUD and the recipe book, on saves in vanilla's format. Worlds from 1.8 to 26.2 are upgraded as vanilla does. [Status table](#project-status). - **Horizon's own extras:** new menus (vanilla's are one setting away), graphics presets, distant terrain up to 1024 chunks, controller support, optional zoom, minimap and more, all off by default where they would change the vanilla look. See [Settings](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/settings). - **Resource packs and data packs:** resource packs work, and data packs load functions, predicates and item modifiers. - **Playing with others:** invite friends from the pause menu's Friends button with a code, Open to LAN, and joining offline-mode servers. Horizon cannot sign in to a Microsoft account yet, so it cannot join servers that check accounts. See [Multiplayer](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/multiplayer). - **Mods:** Horizon has its own mod system (Rust compiled to WebAssembly). Java mod jars do not run. See [Mods and data packs](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/mods). Screenshots, captured in the Rust client itself with vanilla assets and no mods or shaders:
## Host a server The launcher's **Servers** page creates, starts, backs up and updates a Horizon server with buttons, and invites friends over Tailscale. On a VPS, `horizon-server` installs with one command and runs without Java. Guide: [Host a server](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/hosting) ([reference](docs/hosting.md)). ## Modpacks The launcher's **Modpacks** page imports a Modrinth or CurseForge pack, shows which of its mods Horizon can carry over, and plays the ones it can as their own profile. Today that means content mods made of data and assets; mods with Java code are not ported yet. See [Modpacks](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/modpacks). ## Agent control AI agents and scripts can play Horizon. `horizon-ctl`, shipped beside the game in every release folder, is a command line that reads the game as JSON and acts like a player; `horizon-ctl mcp` serves the same commands as an MCP server (one tool per command, screenshots returned as images). ```sh horizon-ctl launch --world Survival --seed 5 --wait # finds the version the launcher installed horizon-ctl state # position, health, food, target, screen... horizon-ctl find-block birch_log # the nearest logs horizon-ctl goto -0.5 65 -2.5 --near 2.5 # walks there along a path horizon-ctl break -1 65 -3 # mines it; replies with the drops horizon-ctl open-inventory && horizon-ctl click-slot 0 # menus: slots, buttons by label, text fields ``` Commands block until the action is done and reply with what happened; errors are JSON with distinct exit codes, `horizon-ctl help` lists every command and `horizon-ctl COMMAND --help` explains one with examples. It talks to the game over a Unix socket on Linux and macOS and over a token-protected localhost port on Windows. See [Agent control in the native client guide](docs/native-client.md#agent-control-horizon-ctl-and-mcp). ## Build from source For developers. Requirements: Rust 1.90 or newer, Python 3.10 or newer, JDK 25, and on Linux the ALSA and udev development headers (`libasound2-dev libudev-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu). Development and the vanilla harnesses run on Linux. Horizon contains no game files and never downloads them. It builds its resources from **your own copy** of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3, verified against the checksums in `research-lock.json`: 1. **Client:** install Java Edition with the official launcher and play 26.3 once. Horizon reads `versions/26.3/`, `libraries/` and `assets/` from the launcher's game directory (`~/.minecraft` on Linux). If yours lives elsewhere, pass `--minecraft-dir` or set `HORIZON_MINECRAFT_DIR`. 2. **Server jar:** the 26.3 server jar, from the `downloads.server.url` in your launcher's `versions/26.3/26.3.json` (or [minecraft.net/download/server](https://www.minecraft.net/en-us/download/server) while 26.3 is the current release). Pass it with `--server-jar` or set `HORIZON_SERVER_JAR`. It is only needed the first time. ```sh git clone https://github.com/ludovic111/horizon.git cd horizon cargo run --release -p horizon-prepare -- --prepare --server-jar ~/Downloads/server.jar # needs JDK 25 cargo run --release -p horizon-prepare -- sounds # optional: sounds from your launcher install cargo run --release -p horizon-client ``` Everything prepared lands in the gitignored `.local/`. It is derived from the game: never commit it or share it. The client starts on the title screen. Command-line options (`--world`, `--seed`, `--creative`, `--render-distance`, `--dedicated`), controls, scripting through `horizon-ctl` and the architecture are described in [the native client guide](docs/native-client.md). The rest of the developer documentation is indexed in [docs/README.md](docs/README.md), including [the parity workflow](docs/parity-workflow.md). ## Roadmap What is being done now, what comes next and where you can help, in plain words and in technical detail: [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md). [playhorizon.dev/hub](https://playhorizon.dev/hub) shows it with the work board, the journal of what shipped and how to help. ## Contributing Issues and pull requests are welcome: see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for how we work (vanilla first, small pull requests, labels), or [the contributing guide](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/contributing) on the site. Questions and ideas: [Discord](https://discord.gg/HcTeMZxe5E). Before opening a pull request, run the self-check and paste the block it prints: ```sh git config core.hooksPath .githooks python3 tools/pr_ready.py ``` It runs rustfmt, clippy with warnings denied, the tests of the crates you touched, the Python tests, the public-tree check, and the vanilla harnesses your change can affect. CI runs the same checks on GitHub's Linux runners; the vanilla harnesses need the game, which Horizon never downloads, so they run on a maintainer's computer holding their own copy. Never commit game files, decompiled source or prepared resources: `tools/check_public_tree.py` rejects them, and tracked Java is allowed only under the project's own `dev/horizonlab` namespace. ## Project status The table below is the project's own audit of each subsystem. Every subsystem now matches vanilla in every harness that compares it. 100% means 100% of what the harnesses compare, not proof that nothing else differs. The remaining known differences are listed below. ### Java parity: 100% Each subsystem scores 0 (absent), 0.25 (started, not playable), 0.5 (playable, major vanilla features missing), 0.75 (playable, mostly complete) or 1 (complete and verified against vanilla by differential tests). The percentage is the average; `tests/test_parity.py` keeps it in sync with this table. Last audited 2026-10-13 against the harness results: all 281 harnesses pass on Linux, each rerun whenever one of its inputs changed, and the Mac mini now runs every one of them too (Rust uses Java's own float maths on each platform). | Subsystem | Score | Main gaps | | --- | ---: | --- | | Window, input and game loop | 1 | None: the game loop, options, camera, auto-jump, toggle sprint/sneak, local input and the frame limiter match vanilla | | Assets and resources | 1 | None: item models match vanilla over 196,290 stacks and the client draws every item through them; the resource pack screen matches vanilla's drawing over 3,000 sessions of clicks, scrolling and searching, its incompatibility confirmation included | | Network protocol and multiplayer | 1 | None: joins vanilla servers; the dedicated server (`--dedicated`) matches vanilla's files, status ping, login, configuration, play, chunks, chat, recipes, advancements and command tree, a client built from vanilla's packet code joins it, Horizon joins a vanilla server, and LAN disco
